value.overview: The Band-tailed Pigeon is a large, powerful pigeon of mountainous forests in the Americas. It has a blue-gray body, a dark tail crossed by a broad pale band, and a conspicuous white crescent on the back of the neck. In Costa Rica it is known as the paloma collareja and occurs mainly in highland forests. It feeds in trees and often travels in flocks, sometimes making a loud wing-clapping sound when it takes flight.
value.classification: The Band-tailed Pigeon belongs to the pigeon and dove family Columbidae. Some modern taxonomic treatments separate southern populations, including birds from Costa Rica, as the Southern Band-tailed Pigeon, Patagioenas albilinea; other references retain them within Patagioenas fasciata.
value.identification: This is a large pigeon, about 33 to 40 cm long, with a rounded head, broad wings, and a longish, square-ended tail. Adults are generally slate-gray or blue-gray above and purplish-gray below. The most useful field mark is the pale gray terminal band across the darker tail, together with the white neck crescent. Costa Rican birds are often darker than northern birds and may have a mostly yellow bill rather than the yellow bill with a dark tip seen in many northern populations.
value.rangeHabitat: The species ranges through western North America, Mexico, Central America, and the mountains of South America, although southern populations may be treated separately by some authorities. In Costa Rica it is primarily associated with forested highlands, generally from about 900 m to the highest ridges, including areas such as the Guanacaste highlands, the Talamancan region, the San Ignacio de Acosta area, and the mountains near San Vito de Coto Brus. It uses mature montane forest, woodland edges, clearings with large trees, and occasionally lower-elevation forest corridors.
value.migrationStatus: In Costa Rica the population is generally considered resident, but birds make local and seasonal elevational movements and may gather in large flocks. Northern populations are more strongly migratory and can move south into Central America during the nonbreeding season; Costa Rica also supports a resident southern population.
value.breeding: Breeding information from Costa Rica is less complete than information from North America. The species generally nests in trees within forest or woodland, placing a loose platform of twigs on a branch. The usual clutch is one white egg, and both adults share incubation and care of the young. Breeding may be influenced by local rainfall and fruit availability. In Costa Rica, nesting is expected mainly in montane forest, but records from lower elevations show that suitable forest corridors can also be used.
value.dietFeeding: Band-tailed Pigeons eat a wide variety of plant material, including fruits, berries, seeds, acorns, grains, and other fleshy or hard forest foods. They usually forage in trees but may descend to the ground or visit open areas when food is available there. The species often moves between feeding sites in flocks and may use mineral-rich soil, mineral springs, or other mineral sources, especially where dietary minerals are limited.
value.behavior: This pigeon is social for much of the year and commonly travels or rests in groups. It has a strong, direct flight and may produce a sharp clapping or cracking sound with its wings during takeoff. Birds often perch high in the canopy, where their subdued plumage can make them difficult to detect. Their calls are low and resonant, and local movements may follow fruiting trees, water sources, and changing food conditions.

conservation.populationTrend: Population trends are mixed and incompletely known. Several monitored North American populations have shown long-term declines, while information from Costa Rica and other parts of the Neotropics is limited; local declines have been reported in some areas.
conservation.threats: Loss, fragmentation, and degradation of montane forest can reduce feeding and nesting habitat. In some parts of its range, hunting pressure and changes in forest structure have also contributed to declines. The status of the Costa Rican population requires better long-term monitoring.
conservation.howToHelp: Protect mature highland forests, forest corridors, and large fruiting trees, including habitat outside formal protected areas. Discourage hunting and disturbance of pigeons at feeding or mineral sites. Support bird monitoring and conservation programs in Costa Rica that document population changes, habitat use, and seasonal movements.
